query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles, premelting is initiated by the selective surface segregation of copper. Copper’s lower melting point and relatively weaker bonds drive its diffusion to the nanoparticle surface, forming a Cu-rich layer that locally melts at lower temperatures, thereby depressing the overall melting point. This effect is amplified in smaller particles due to their higher surface‐to‐volume ratios.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles prepared under conditions that yield homogeneous solid solutions with minimal macroscopic phase separation. Nanoparticles should be synthesized in a controlled size range (e.g., 5–50 nm).
generation.intervention: Subject the nanoparticles to a controlled thermal ramp (in an inert atmosphere) across the premelting and melting regime while monitoring structural and compositional evolution in situ (using high-resolution TEM or neutron imaging combined with elemental mapping).
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under inert gas to prevent oxidation; controlled heating from just below the onset of premelting (around 1050°C) to full melting (up to ~1450°C) at a sufficiently slow rate to allow equilibrium surface diffusion. Nanoparticles with systematically varied sizes will be compared.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a Cu-rich surface layer (via surface segregation) acts as the structural mediator that triggers the onset of localized melting (premelting) at lower temperatures.
generation.mechanism: Due to copper’s intrinsically lower melting point relative to Fe, Ni, Cr, and Co, its atoms become mobile earlier upon heating and preferentially migrate to the nanoparticle surface. In nanoparticles, the high surface-to-volume ratio amplifies this segregation, causing local regions of premelted copper. These areas serve as nucleation sites for the melting of the entire particle, thus lowering the effective melting temperature as particle size decreases.
generation.predicted_outcome: In-situ imaging and elemental mapping will reveal the emergence of a Cu-rich layer on the nanoparticle surfaces at temperatures noticeably below the bulk melting point. Smaller nanoparticles will show a greater depression in their overall melting temperatures compared to larger ones, correlating with more pronounced surface segregation.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles of similar composition but larger sizes (or reference alloys where Cu is replaced by a higher-melting-point metal) are expected to exhibit higher melting onset temperatures with less pronounced premelting behavior.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles within the temperature range relevant to premelting and melting (approximately 1050°C to 1450°C) and in particles small enough (≤50 nm) for surface effects to dominate. The hypothesis may not extend to bulk samples or systems with drastically different elemental ratios or under ultra-rapid cooling conditions that suppress equilibrium segregation.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal combines observations from in-situ neutron imaging studies (PMC8320920) that report surface Cu phase formation and MD simulations (PMC6479918) showing size‐dependent melting point depression in nanocrystalline HEAs. The novel aspect is extending these ideas to the FeNiCrCoCu system to explicitly link Cu surface segregation with a lowered and size-dependent melting point. Uncertainties remain regarding the kinetics of Cu diffusion in these complex nanoparticles and the quantitative temperature offset induced by the segregated layer.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles with controlled diameters (e.g., 5 nm, 20 nm, and 50 nm) and perform in-situ heating experiments (using TEM or neutron imaging) under inert conditions. Acquire real-time elemental maps (via EDX or equivalent) and record the temperature at which a Cu-rich layer forms compared to the onset of bulk melting.
measurements: Temperature at which a Cu-rich surface layer is detected
Overall melting temperature of nanoparticles as a function of size
Correlation between the extent of surface segregation and melting temperature depression
Comparison of the melting behavior with that of larger particles or a variant composition lacking Cu segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant Cu segregation is detected prior to melting, or if the measured melting temperatures do not decrease with diminishing particle size, then the hypothesized mechanism is not supported. Additionally, if replacing Cu with another low-melting-point element does not yield a similar depression in melting behavior, the hypothesis would be decisively falsified.

The CoCrCuNi alloy has been previously shown to solidify into a uniform dendritic microstructure from arc-melting [], which is indicative that the microstructure evolved from a single-phase liquid as opposed to the large-scale macroscopic-phase separation that has been observed in similar alloys of CoCrCu [] and CoCrCuFe []. However, there are no reported slow cooling solidification studies on the CoCrCuNi alloy. Previous neutron imaging of the CoCrCu by the present authors resulted in neutron radiographs of the CoCrCu displaying the buttons melting and separating based on density []. The stacking of the liquid immiscible phases of CoCr-rich liquid and Cu-rich liquid was characterized by their differences in neutron attenuation. The same experiment was essentially repeated for this work with the equiatomic addition of Ni buttons such that the equiatomic CoCrCu becomes equiatomic CoCrCuNi once melting and dissolution has occurred. This allows for a more equilibrium solidification due to the slow cooling, as well as an opportunity to image the remixing of the immiscible CoCr-rich and Cu-rich liquid phases.
